source.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization
source.authors: Collin Burns; Pavel Izmailov; J. Kirchner; Bowen Baker; Leo Gao; Leopold Aschenbrenner; Yining Chen; Adrien Ecoffet; Manas R. Joglekar; Jan Leike; I. Sutskever; Jeff Wu

record.tranche_reason: This is the original study: it fine-tunes strong pretrained models on weak-model labels and reports performance gap recovered.
record.gate_note: Included reported weak-to-strong outcomes and method comparisons that bear on the claim. Did not extract individual values visible only in plots where the text gives no corresponding value; results from cited work are excluded.
record.test_reason: This is the original source. It fine-tunes GPT-4-family students on weak-model labels and reports PGR across NLP, chess and reward modelling, with method variants and an ImageNet vision experiment. Because it is the original source for every version, no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Naive fine-tuning on weak labels consistently beats the weak supervisor but recovers only part of the gap, and does poorly on ChatGPT reward modelling. Simple methods help in some settings but none works universally: the confidence loss mainly on NLP, bootstrapping mainly on chess, generative fine-tuning on RM. The authors flag imitation saliency and pretraining leakage as disanalogies that may make results optimistic.
record.recipe_differences: The core baseline follows the original weak-to-strong procedure: generate labels with a weaker model, fine-tune a stronger pretrained model, and compare with weak and ground-truth-trained performance. The paper also tests auxiliary losses, bootstrapping, generative fine-tuning, linear probes, and other variants.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by task, weak-supervisor and strong-student size, weak-label error structure, and training method. The confidence loss is less helpful for small gaps and some inverse-scaling datasets; chess PGR declines with student size, unlike the stated NLP trend.

fits_no_version.finding: Easy-to-hard generalization: ground-truth training on easy chess puzzles or easy NLP examples, evaluated on hard ones (Appendix C, Figs 19–22). On hard puzzles, chess performance matches zero-shot.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on easy examples with correct labels generalizes to hard examples.

record.problems: The ChatGPT reward-model dataset is proprietary. Several comparisons and trends are presented mainly in plots, with limited numerical detail in the text. The authors note that ground-truth early stopping uses information unavailable in a valid method and that best test accuracy may be overstated due to noisy evaluations. They also identify pretraining leakage and weak imitation of supervisor errors as disanalogies that may make results optimistic for future superhuman supervision.
record.rows_left_out: No result-bearing rows omitted under the 60-row limit. More granular figure-only values, including individual model-pair curves, were not extracted where the text did not state their values.

untested.parts: Ensembling weak supervisors is not tested.

Two parts are not tested: PGR under distribution shift between training and test, and strong students exploiting what the supervisor cannot check (no RL optimisation against the learned reward model).
No theoretical conditions are derived or tested.
Vision is tested only with an AlexNet supervisor and two DINO linear-probe students on ImageNet.

missing.what: Student-supervisor agreement shows inverse scaling: larger students agree less with supervisor errors, across NLP, chess and RM. The confidence loss reduces agreement on supervisor mistakes.
Few-shot prompting with weak labels does worse than with ground-truth labels. For the largest students it is competitive with naive fine-tuning but below the confidence loss.
Chess students trained with much weaker supervisors sometimes fall below the zero-shot baseline of the same size.
With the confidence loss, the PGR boost from ground-truth early stopping shrinks from about 15% to about 5%. This shows the loss reduces overfitting to weak labels.

Many methods gave negative or no gains: LP-FT, weight decay/dropout, LoRA, data augmentation, generalized cross-entropy, label noise, weight averaging. Confidence thresholding helped only with very poor weak labels (about 60% accuracy). The product confidence loss gave small positive gains on two tasks.
Generative fine-tuning applied to both supervisors and students also raises PGR.
Weak-to-strong results in the linear-probing setting qualitatively match fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: This is the original source for all versions, so no verdict labels are assigned. Rows r13 and r14 are ground-truth early-stopping oracles, not valid methods. Row r17 is a deliberately induced imitation condition, still useful as V4 evidence on error simulatability. r20 and r21 values check against Table 3: (60.7−56.6)/(63.7−56.6)=57.7% and (64.2−56.6)/(74.9−56.6)=41.5%.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests the effect across its own tasks and GPT-4-family models, not every model or task.
It tests selected training changes, not ensembling weak supervisors.
It studies GPT-4-family model sizes, NLP, chess and reward modeling, plus an ImageNet vision experiment; it does not establish general scaling laws or a comprehensive account of predictors.
It studies weak-error structures and an explicit imitation condition, but does not test the claim's distribution-shift condition.
No theoretical condition under which a student must beat its supervisor is derived or tested.
Vision is tested on ImageNet with AlexNet and DINO models only.

source_check.correct: State: observed for the error-structure dependence. Matched-accuracy labelers yield widely differing generalization; easy-to-fit errors induce faster overfitting, whereas random errors often permit continued improvement.

source_check.notes: Original source; no verdict labels apply. Statement checks cover this study only; other studies and synthesis-wide counts were not independently checked. Appendix E.1 students are logistic-regression probes on frozen representations from one intermediate-sized GPT-4-family model.

statements.correction: Section 5.1.1: ground-truth early stopping improves NLP PGR by 15 percentage points over the final checkpoint. Appendix E.3, Figure 27: explicitly providing the weak label in the prompt yields baseline average PGR 0.002 ± 0.003.
statements.problem: Both numerical results are correct, but appending the weak label tests imitation saliency, not training duration or early stopping.

statements.correction: Appendix E: synthetic error-structure and imitation experiments. Sections 5.1.1–5.1.2, Figures 7–8 and 13: overfitting and imitation of actual weak supervisors' errors. Section 4.1: no RL optimization against the reward model.
statements.problem: The description of the original's failure-mode evidence as exclusively synthetic omits its measurements of overfitting and imitation with ordinary weak-model labels.
